A member of the board risk committee at a Brazilian bank receives a BRL model-governance paper explaining why the bank is replacing its Vasicek model. The paper contains four statements about the Vasicek model:

I. Calibrating the model to match one point on the term structure relies too heavily on the model to approximate all other points.

II. A single factor explains a large fraction of term structure variability, particularly across shorter maturities, so one factor suffices to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds.

III. The model cannot capture the empirical regularity that the term structure of volatility rises quickly with term and then flattens or declines, so it cannot simultaneously handle options spread across the term structure.

IV. The single volatility parameter can be used to approximate an implied option volatility at one point of the term structure.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: I, III and IV only
options.D: II, III and IV only

2. One factor is not enough: “while one factor does explain a lot of term structure variability, a second factor can capture significantly more variability. More than one factor is needed to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds.”
3. No volatility hump: it “cannot capture the empirical regularity . . . that the term structure of volatilities . . . typically rises quickly with term and then flattens or declines”, so it cannot “simultaneously handle options or other volatility-sensitive products that are spread out across the term structure”.

question:
The treasurer of a Canadian credit union hedged a CAD 250 million long position in 3-year notes by selling 10-year government bonds, using DV01 ratios from a Vasicek model fitted to the curve. Over a quarter in which markets repriced expected central bank policy, 2- to 3-year yields rose 45 bp while 10-year yields rose 8 bp, and the hedged position lost heavily. Which of the following best explains the failure and the remedy?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.A: $\sigma$ was calibrated to the 10-year point; recalibrating $\sigma$ to the 3-year implied volatility would make the single-factor hedge ratio reliable.
options.B: One factor cannot reliably hedge bonds sensitive to one curve segment with bonds sensitive to another; intermediate and shorter bonds need a multifactor model such as Gauss+.
options.C: The Vasicek model has no mean reversion, so it assumed that the 10-year bond would move one-for-one with the 3-year note; adding mean reversion fixes the ratio.
options.D: One factor cannot reliably hedge bonds sensitive to one curve segment with bonds sensitive to another; Gauss+ fixes this by adding a random shock to the short rate.

solution:
**Case: a single-factor hedge across curve segments**

Stem in one line: 3-year notes hedged with 10-year bonds on Vasicek DV01s; 2 to 3-year yields up 45 bp, 10-year up 8 bp; why it failed.

**Concept and theory**

A one-factor model has one sensitivity shape, $e^{-kt}$, linking every rate to every other. A hedge between two maturities works only if the market moves them in that fixed ratio. When the curve moves in a way that is not a multiple of $e^{-kt}$ (for example, the 2- to 3-year sector reprices on central bank expectations while the 10-year stays put), the hedge breaks. GARP: Vasicek cannot “reliably hedge bonds most sensitive to one segment of the term structure with bonds most sensitive to another segment”, and “more than one factor is needed to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds.” Gauss+ has three factors, and a medium-term factor that reflects business cycles and monetary policy, so exposures to different segments can be hedged separately.

**Applying it to this question**

The loss came from a non-parallel, segment-specific move that a single-factor DV01 ratio cannot represent. The CAD 250 million size and the exact basis points only describe the damage. The remedy is more factors, not a different $\sigma$.

**Fragile fact.** Single-factor hedges fail across segments; fixing $\sigma$ does not help because hedge ratios depend on $k$.

question:
A risk consultant at a US asset manager is building a USD factor-exposure report and compares how forward rates of different terms respond to a change in each model’s factor or factors, using the estimated Gauss+ model described in the reading. Which of the following comparisons is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.A: Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the medium-term factor dominates forward rates beyond 10 years, and the long-term factor drives mainly the 2- to 3-year part of the curve.
options.B: Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the long-term factor has its largest impact at the very short end, and its effect fades steadily beyond 10 years.
options.C: Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the short-term factor affects only the very short end, the medium-term factor drives mainly the 2- to 3-year part, and the long-term factor alone drives terms beyond 10 years.
options.D: Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the short-term factor, being the policy rate, moves forward rates of all terms by similar amounts, while $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ add only small corrections.

solution:
**Forward-rate sensitivities to the factors**

Stem in one line: which statement correctly contrasts how forward rates respond to the factor(s) in each model?

**Concept and theory**

Vasicek: one factor, one shape. The sensitivity of $f$ ($t$) to $r$ is $e^{-kt}$, declining smoothly with term (GARP §16.1).

Gauss+: each factor has its own footprint on the curve. From GARP’s description of Figure 16.7 (estimated model):

| Factor | Effect on forward rates |
|---|---|
| Short-term rate $r_{t}$ | Affects only the very short end of the curve |
| Medium-term factor $m_{t}$ | Drives the 2- to 3-year part; captures where the market believes the short rate will be in two to three years (monetary policy) |
| Long-term factor $l_{t}$ | Biggest impact at 6 to 8 years; beyond 10 years, the sole factor driving forward rate changes and volatilities |

GARP also explains the mechanism: the larger $\alpha_{r}$, the faster changes in $m$ and $l$ reach the curve; the larger $\alpha_{m}$, the faster $m$ converges to $l$ and the less $m$ affects longer yields; the smaller $\alpha_{l}$, the more parallel the effect of $l$ on all longer yields.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options give Vasicek correctly; the discrimination is the segment assigned to each Gauss+ factor. Only C matches Figure 16.7.

question:
The head of rates strategy at a UK asset manager proposes a GBP strategy. Using a fitted Gauss+ model, the team will estimate the market-implied long-run expectation of the short rate as the 10-year forward rate minus a term-appropriate risk premium plus a term-appropriate convexity, compare it with an economist’s fundamental estimate of the long-run rate, and buy or sell long-dated bonds outright on the gap. *Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.A: It is a relative value trade, because the position is structured to be hedged against changes in the medium- and long-term factors.
options.B: It is a macro trade, and the Gauss+ model separates expectations from risk premium using observed bond prices alone, with no extra assumption.
options.C: It is a macro trade, and when rates fall and the curve steepens, the model interprets the steepening as a fall in the risk premium.
options.D: It is a macro trade, and separating expectations from risk premium relies on assuming that short-rate expectations stop changing beyond some future date.

solution:
**Case: a macro trade on the long-run rate**

Stem in one line: estimate the market-implied long-run short rate with Gauss+, compare it with an economist’s view, and trade long bonds outright on the gap.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two uses of Gauss+ for proprietary trading:

- Relative value: find value “in the absence of factor exposure”.
- Macro trading: “takes direct or indirect views on the factors”. A more complex example is “trying to trade the long-run level of the short-term rate”.

Long-term forward rates combine expectations, risk premium and convexity; convexity is easy to compute, but separating expectations from risk premium is hard (in Vasicek, impossible from prices, Q8). GARP’s method “relies on one key assumption: expectations of future short-term rates do not change past some point in the future”. The long-run expectation is then the 10-year forward rate minus the term-appropriate risk premium plus the term-appropriate convexity. The gap to an exogenous fundamental view (GARP uses the Cleveland Fed) “can be used as a basis for taking outright long or short positions in bonds.” “The risk premium often moves in the opposite direction of rates. I. If $r_{t} < m_{t}$, the change in the short-term rate over the step is positive, whatever the levels of $l_{t}$ and $\mu$.

II. If $m_{t} > l_{t}$, the change in the medium-term factor over the step is negative, even when $l_{t}$ is below $\mu$.

III. If $l_{t} > \mu$, the change in the long-term factor over the step is positive, because the long-term factor is the slowest to revert.

IV. If $r_{t} > m_{t}$ but $r_{t} < \mu$, the change in the short-term rate over the step is positive, because the short-term rate ultimately reverts to $\mu$.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: I and IV only
options.D: II, III and IV only

solution:
**Sign of each factor’s drift**

Stem in one line: which statements about the sign of each factor’s one-step change (shocks set to zero) are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

With the shocks at zero, each factor’s change is its drift only:

∆$r$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt,$ ∆$m$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt,$ ∆$l$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt.$

Each $\alpha$ is positive, so the sign of each change is the sign of that factor’s own gap to its own target, reversed: a factor above its target falls, a factor below its target rises. The targets are, in order, $m$ for $r$, $l$ for $m$ and $\mu$ for $l$. Schweser: “rt is seeking to converge to mt, which is trying to converge to lt, which is trying to converge to $\mu$. Note that the only fixed parameter here is $\mu$, while the other factors are dynamically moving targets.”

| Factor | Target | Speed | Shock in its own equation |
|---|---|---|---|
| $r$ | $m$ | $\alpha_{r}$ (fastest) | none |
| $m$ | $l$ | $\alpha_{m}$ | $\sigma_{m}$($\rho dW^{1}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}$) |
| $l$ | $\mu$ (fixed) | $\alpha_{l}$ (slowest) | $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}$ |

The speed only scales the size of the move; it never changes its sign.

options.D: Reorder so that the mean reversion parameters come first from the regression coefficients, which depend only on them; then fit $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ and $\rho$; then estimate $\mu$.

solution:
**Order of the estimation stages**

Stem in one line: a bank fits volatilities before mean reversion speeds; which regulatory finding is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The order of the stages is not arbitrary; it follows the dependence structure.

| Step | Estimates | Why it can be done at this point |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | $r$ series | Observed: fed funds target (proxy for policy rate) |
| 1 | $\alpha_{r}, \alpha_{m}, \alpha_{l}$ | Regression coefficients depend only on the speeds, so no other parameter is needed |
| 2 | $\sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}, \rho$ | Fitted to the volatility term structure given the speeds; mean reversion shapes how $\sigma$’s become yield volatilities |
| 3 | $\mu$ | “The last remaining parameter”; least squares on yield levels over the whole sample |

Schweser lists the same order as Steps 1 to 6.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank’s step 2 needs mean reversion values it has not yet estimated, so its volatility estimates rest on provisional speeds. The reading’s order removes this problem: speeds first (they need nothing else), then volatilities and correlation, then $\mu$. Option D states this order and the reason for it.

**Fragile fact.** Speeds, then volatilities and correlation, then $\mu$. The regressions do not need volatilities; the reverse is not claimed.

question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian bank has run the first stage of a Gauss+ estimation on CAD zero-coupon yields, regressing daily changes in zero yields of various terms on daily changes in the two-year and 10-year zero yields. Two of the results are:

| Regressed yield | Coefficient on 2-year yield | Coefficient on 10-year yield |
|---|---|---|
| 4-year | 0.84 | 0.29 |
| 20-year | −0.17 | 1.12 |

Which of the following interpretations is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: $r$, $m$ and $l$ are the short-term rate, the medium-term factor and the long-term factor; $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$, $\alpha_{l}$ are their mean reversion parameters; $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ are the volatility parameters of $m$ and $l$; $\rho$ is the correlation between the shocks to $m$ and $l$; $\mu$ is the constant to which $l$ reverts.

options.A: The coefficients implicitly describe the mean reversion parameters, and this stage chooses $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$ and $\alpha_{l}$ so that the model-implied coefficients match them as closely as possible.
options.B: The coefficients are direct estimates of the loadings of yields on the factors, because in the model $m$ equals the two-year yield and $l$ equals the 10-year yield.
options.C: The negative coefficient of the 20-year yield on the two-year yield signals misspecification, so this stage should restrict all coefficients to be non-negative.
options.D: The coefficients feed the volatility stage: $\sigma_{m}$ is set from the coefficients on the two-year yield and $\sigma_{l}$ from the coefficients on the 10-year yield.

solution:
**Reading the stage 1 regression coefficients**

Stem in one line: 4-year yield loads 0.84/0.29 and 20-year loads −0.17/1.12 on 2y/10y changes; most accurate interpretation?

**Concept and theory**

The regressions summarize how the whole curve moves with two anchor yields. A short-intermediate yield (here 4 years) moves mostly with the two-year yield; a long yield (20 years) moves mostly, even more than one for one, with the 10-year yield, and can load negatively on the two-year yield once the 10-year move is controlled for. GARP’s own results have the same pattern (three-year: 0.91 and 0.22; 15-year: −0.20 and 1.10). GARP: “all these regression coefficients implicitly describe the mean reversion parameters of the model. This stage of the estimation, therefore, chooses the parameters $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$ and $\alpha_{l}$ so that the model captures the empirically observed regression coefficients as closely as possible.” The model reproduces these coefficients, including the negative one, “within statistical confidence intervals”.

**Applying it to this question**

The coefficients are data that the model’s speeds must reproduce. They are not factor loadings, not volatility inputs, and the negative sign is a feature of the data that the model matches.
